headline: High risk of prompt injection and data leakage: aci’s broad CRM/email/network access can feed LangGraph’s writable, browser-capable orchestration pipeline.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: aci can ingest and emit CRM/email/research content, and LangGraph can route node outputs through a graph with no self-isolation. If aci content is passed into LangGraph nodes or tools, prompt-like instructions in shared files or messages could steer execution. The pathway is plausible in default orchestration, though not proven by docs alone.
conditions: IF aci outputs are fed into LangGraph node prompts or tool inputs without sanitization
IF a shared workspace or message queue carries aci-generated text into LangGraph
mitigations: Add an instruction/content delimiter around aci outputs
Strip or escape tool directives before passing text onward
Insert a verification node that classifies content as data vs instructions
Use separate channels for human text and machine control
requires-engineering: add provenance tags end-to-end

B_data_leakage.rationale: aci touches email, CRM, calendar, support, and research data and has broad network egress; LangGraph can read/write application-defined files and call model providers. If aci data enters LangGraph state, it can be persisted or forwarded to third-party APIs, creating a realistic exfiltration path with sensitive business data in default deployments.
conditions: IF aci data is stored in LangGraph state or application-defined files
IF LangGraph nodes send that state to model providers or developer-defined tools
mitigations: Minimize fields copied from aci into graph state
Redact email/CRM payloads before persistence
Disable logging of full node inputs and outputs
Store secrets in a separate vault, not graph state
requires-engineering: enforce per-field data classification

C_capability_conflict.rationale: aci can make broad API calls and LangGraph can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, read/write files, and use browser tools. Their capabilities overlap on mutable external resources, so concurrent instances can race or overwrite shared application state unless the orchestrator adds locking. The conflict is plausible but not inherently destructive from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF both agents target the same CRM, file, or API record set
IF multiple LangGraph instances share the same checkpointer store
mitigations: Serialize writes to shared records
Use per-run namespaces for files and keys
Add optimistic concurrency checks on updates
Disable parallel writes for overlapping workflows
requires-engineering: introduce distributed locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: aci can generate CRM/email/calendar actions and LangGraph is a general orchestrator that can execute downstream tools and browser actions. If LangGraph treats aci output as authoritative, a mistaken or malicious aci result can cascade into real-world actions such as emails, CRM updates, or shell commands. The pair therefore has a strong default automation hazard.
conditions: IF LangGraph uses aci output as direct tool arguments or final decisions
IF no human or rule-based verification step exists before action execution
mitigations: Require a confirmation step before external actions
Validate aci outputs against schemas and allowlists
Show diffs for any email/CRM/calendar mutation
Block shell/browser actions unless a policy node approves
requires-engineering: add confidence-based gating

E_compliance.rationale: aci handles email, CRM, calendar, and customer support data, while LangGraph can persist graph state and send data to model providers. That creates a plausible retention/residency mismatch if regulated customer data is copied into graph state or provider calls. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction breach, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is copied from aci into LangGraph state
IF model-provider calls retain prompts or outputs beyond the source system policy
mitigations: Classify regulated fields before orchestration
Keep compliance-sensitive data out of graph state
Review provider retention settings
Document data-flow boundaries for operators
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
